meta.title: Who originally recorded "Sway"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Dean Martin’s 1954 Capitol hit was a cover of the Mexican song “¿Quién será?”. The earliest documented recording is a 1953 Seeco 78 by La Sonora Matancera with Nelson Pinedo; the often-repeated 1953 Pablo Beltrán Ruiz instrumental is unsourced.
meta.ogDescription: Not Dean Martin. The song is the Mexican “¿Quién será?”, and the earliest documented recording is a 1953 Seeco 78 by La Sonora Matancera with Nelson Pinedo.

answer.label: Not a Dean Martin original — the Mexican song “¿Quién será?”, earliest documented on a 1953 Seeco 78 by La Sonora Matancera with Nelson Pinedo
answer.originalArtist: La Sonora Matancera with Nelson Pinedo
answer.originalArtistDates: La Sonora Matancera, Cuban conjunto founded 1924 in Matanzas · Nelson Pinedo, Colombian singer, 1928-2016
answer.sourceLine: Dean Martin’s 1954 Capitol single is so completely the version people carry around that the song reads as his invention. It isn’t. The song is a Mexican bolero-mambo called “¿Quién será?”, written by Luis Demetrio and Pablo Beltrán Ruiz, and it was on record in Spanish before Martin sang a note of it. Which record came first is genuinely contested: SecondHandSongs, the discography that specialises in first recordings, names the Seeco 78 by La Sonora Matancera with Nelson Pinedo, and Discogs dates that shellac to 1953. English Wikipedia instead says Pablo Beltrán Ruiz’s orchestra cut an instrumental cha-cha-chá in 1953 — a sentence with no citation, and SecondHandSongs dates that performance to 1959, on the RCA LP the article says it was “later included on”. What is not in doubt is the direction of travel: Norman Gimbel’s English lyric, written in 1954, is a different text on the same tune, and the Spanish original quietly disappeared from the English-speaking record of the song.

original.released: The earliest documented issue of the song is a Seeco 78rpm shellac of “¿Quién será?” by La Sonora Matancera with Nelson Pinedo singing, dated 1953 by Discogs and named the original version by SecondHandSongs. Treat the year as the best-supported date rather than a settled one: English Wikipedia dates Pinedo’s arrival in the group to 1954, and a competing claim puts a Pablo Beltrán Ruiz instrumental first in the same year.
original.charted: No English-language chart placing. It circulated in Cuba, Mexico and the rest of Latin America; the song’s Spanish-language fame came instead through Pedro Infante, who sang it in a 1954 film.

trail: SecondHandSongs, which tracks originals and covers as its whole purpose, carries the composition as “Quién será” by Pablo Beltrán Ruiz and Luis Demetrio ↗ and names the Sonora Matancera performance with Nelson Pinedo, 1953, as the original version — while dating the Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su orquesta performance to 1959, on the album South of the Border Cha-Cha-Cha.
Discogs independently dates the shellac — “¿Quien Sera? / El Ermitaño”, Seeco 7351, 10-inch 78rpm, 1953 ↗.

UCLA’s Frontera archive holds the same coupling as a physical artefact — “Quien Sera”, Sonora Matancera, vocal Nelson Pinedo, Seeco 509, matrix SR-8168 ↗, catalogued as a bolero-mambo composed by Pablo Beltrán Ruiz. The catalogue entry carries no date.

The competing claim comes from one uncited sentence: Wikipedia states that Pablo Beltrán Ruiz recorded the first version in 1953 as an instrumental cha-cha-chá ↗, later included on the LP South of the Border / Al sur de la frontera. No primary source, catalogue number or trade listing has been found for a 1953 issue, and the discographies date that LP to the end of the decade.

One honest wrinkle on the other side: Wikipedia dates Nelson Pinedo’s arrival in La Sonora Matancera to 1954 ↗, which sits awkwardly against a 1953 pressing. Both candidate firsts are dated 1953 by their best source and questioned by another — which is why this page is marked attributed rather than verified.

MusicBrainz carries the composition as a Spanish-language work credited to both writers — “¿Quién será?”, Luis Demetrio and Pablo Beltrán Ruiz ↗, with the later English recordings attached as performances of it.

authors.name: La Sonora Matancera with Nelson Pinedo
authors.heading: La Sonora Matancera with Nelson Pinedo
authors.metaLine: Cuban conjunto founded 1924 · Nelson Pinedo, Colombian singer, 1928-2016 · Seeco, 1953
authors.bio: La Sonora Matancera formed in Matanzas, Cuba in 1924 and spent the 1950s as the house band of Latin American popular music, signed to Seeco Records from 1949 and cycling a series of guest singers through the front line. Nelson Pinedo, a Colombian from Barranquilla, was one of them, and it is his vocal on the Seeco 78 of “¿Quién será?” that SecondHandSongs names as the original version of the song and Discogs dates to 1953. The date is not airtight — Wikipedia puts Pinedo’s arrival in the group a year later — but it is the earliest issue of the song anyone has produced a catalogue number for.

authors.name: Dean Martin
authors.heading: Dean Martin
authors.metaLine: American singer and actor, 1917-1995 · Capitol Records, 1954
authors.bio: Martin recorded “Sway” for Capitol in 1954 with Dick Stabile’s orchestra, backed with “Money Burns a Hole in My Pocket.” It reached number 15 on the Billboard best-seller chart and number six in the UK, and his easy, half-amused delivery is the reason the song has never left circulation. Nothing about the record is a fault — it is simply a cover, sung in English to a new lyric, of a Mexican song that was already on shellac in Spanish.

authors.name: Luis Demetrio
authors.heading: Luis Demetrio
authors.bio: Demetrio wrote the song with Pedro Infante in mind, and by his own account Pablo Beltrán Ruiz supplied only its opening musical material while he composed the rest and the Spanish lyric. Because Demetrio sold his rights to Beltrán Ruiz, the song has often been credited to Beltrán Ruiz alone — which is how the writer of the song ended up the harder of the two names to find on a label.

authors.name: Pablo Beltrán Ruiz
authors.heading: Pablo Beltrán Ruiz
authors.bio: Beltrán Ruiz led one of the busiest Mexican dance orchestras of the 1950s and wrote music for films starring Pedro Infante, Tin Tan and Cantinflas. He is credited as co-composer of “¿Quién será?” and, after buying Demetrio’s rights, often as its sole author. He is also widely named as its first recording artist, on the strength of an uncited claim that his orchestra cut an instrumental cha-cha-chá version in 1953 — but SecondHandSongs dates that performance to 1959 and no 1953 pressing of it has been documented, so this page does not present him as the original recorder.

authors.name: Norman Gimbel
authors.heading: Norman Gimbel
authors.bio: Gimbel wrote an entirely new English lyric in 1954 under the title “Sway”. It is not a translation: the Spanish text is a wistful one about wondering whether love will come again, and Gimbel replaced it with a dancefloor address to a partner. Same tune, different song — and a different title, which is most of the reason English-speaking listeners never traced it back.

misattribution.heading: Right song, wrong origin story
misattribution.intro: “Sway” is treated in the English-speaking world as a Dean Martin invention. It is a Mexican song that already existed, under a different title, in a different language, with an entirely different lyric.

items.why: His Capitol single with Dick Stabile’s orchestra is the version that charted in the US and UK and the one every later cover answers to. Nothing on the record signals a Spanish-language source.

items.who: La Sonora Matancera with Nelson Pinedo, Seeco, 1953.
items.why: SecondHandSongs names this the original version of “¿Quién será?” and Discogs dates the Seeco 78 to 1953; UCLA’s Frontera archive holds the disc with its catalogue and matrix numbers. It is the earliest issue of the song anyone can point at.

items.who: Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta, instrumental cha-cha-chá, 1953.
items.why: Widely repeated, and traceable to a single uncited sentence on Wikipedia. SecondHandSongs dates that orchestra’s performance to 1959 and Discogs puts the LP it appears on at the end of the 1950s. Until a 1953 pressing turns up, it is a claim, not a date.

items.who: Luis Demetrio and Pablo Beltrán Ruiz; Norman Gimbel wrote the separate English lyric.
items.why: Demetrio wrote the song for Pedro Infante and said Beltrán Ruiz contributed only its opening material — but Demetrio sold his rights to Beltrán Ruiz, so credit has often gone to Beltrán Ruiz alone. Gimbel’s 1954 English words are a new text, not a translation.

misattribution.truthLine: Dean Martin sang it second, in a language and with a lyric the song did not start out in.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: The usual story of an eclipsed original is that a bigger star made a louder record. Here something sharper happened: the English version isn’t a translation. Norman Gimbel wrote a fresh lyric about dancing and attraction over a Mexican song whose Spanish words were melancholy and searching — and gave it a new title. Once a song is called “Sway” in English, there is nothing left in it pointing back to “¿Quién será?”, and no reason for an English-speaking listener to go looking.

The Spanish side of the song is crowded enough that even there no single record settled the question. A Seeco 78 by La Sonora Matancera with Nelson Pinedo is the earliest issue anyone has documented; Pablo Beltrán Ruiz’s orchestra is widely said to have cut an instrumental first, though the discographies date that performance years later; and Luis Demetrio had written the song for Pedro Infante, who sang it in a 1954 film and made it his own across Latin America. So the song split into several lives — and only the English one travelled.
detailsBody: 1953 — La Sonora Matancera, with Nelson Pinedo singing, record “¿Quién será?” for Seeco; the 78 (Seeco 7351, also catalogued as 509) is the earliest documented issue of the song, and SecondHandSongs designates it the original version.

1953, disputed — Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta are said to have recorded an instrumental cha-cha-chá version. The claim is uncited; SecondHandSongs dates that performance to 1959, on the RCA Victor LP South of the Border / Al sur de la frontera – Cha-cha-cha.
1954 — Pedro Infante, the singer Luis Demetrio originally wrote the song for, performs it in the film Escuela de vagabundos (School for Tramps); it becomes one of his signature songs.
1954 — Norman Gimbel writes an unrelated English lyric titled “Sway.” Dean Martin records it for Capitol with Dick Stabile’s orchestra; it reaches number 15 in the US and number six in the UK.
1999 and 2004 — Shaft’s “(Mucho Mambo) Sway” and Michael Bublé’s revival for 143/Reprise reintroduce the song to two more generations, both by way of the English lyric.
context.pull: It wasn’t translated. It was replaced.

schema.faqAnswer: No. Dean Martin's 1954 Capitol record is a cover, sung to a new English lyric by Norman Gimbel. The song is the Mexican "¿Quién será?", written by Luis Demetrio and Pablo Beltrán Ruiz; its earliest documented recording is a 1953 Seeco 78 by La Sonora Matancera with Nelson Pinedo, and a widely repeated but unsourced claim credits a 1953 instrumental by Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta.
